title: Observation of Magnetic-Anisotropy Crossover and High-Temperature Skyrmions in the Dirac Magnet Fe3Ge with a Distorted Kagome Lattice
authors: Yalei Huang, Xiaowei Lv, Bin Li, Chunqiang Xu, Dhanarajagopal Alltrin, Xiaoxuan Ma, Wanting Yang, Wei Zhou, Xiangzhuo Xing, Wen-Chin Lin, Raman Sankar, Michael Smidman, Shixun Cao, Dong Qian, Renchao Che, Xiaofeng Xu
abstract: Topological materials that simultaneously host robust high-temperature skyrmions and nontrivial electronic band structures have attracted tremendous interest owing to their distinctive advantages for both fundamental research and prospective technological applications. Here, we report the observation of robust skyrmions in the Dirac kagome magnet Fe3Ge, which exhibits a high Curie temperature of ~ 650 K. At room temperature, Fe3Ge shows a large intrinsic anomalous Hall conductivity of ~ 380 Ω-1cm-1, originating from its nontrivial electronic band topology. Systematic magnetization measurements reveal a spin reorientation transition at ~ 375 K, indicating a crossover from easy-plane to easy-axis magnetic anisotropy. Below the spin reorientation temperature, a large topological Hall effect is observed, arising from microscopic noncoplanar spin structures. Lorentz transmission electron microscopy shows that mesoscopic skyrmions are stabilized in the easy-axis magnetic anisotropy regime and persist over an exceptionally wide temperature window of 375-650 K, far exceeding that of most previously reported skyrmion-hosting materials. These results establish Fe3Ge as a promising platform for exploring diverse topological properties, with strong potential for advancing future high-temperature spintronic applications, ranging from next-generation information storage to logic computing devices.
summary: This work reports on the discovery of robust, high-temperature skyrmions in the Dirac magnet Fe3Ge. The material exhibits a unique combination of a high Curie temperature, large intrinsic anomalous Hall effect, and a temperature-dependent magnetic anisotropy crossover. By combining advanced transport measurements with LTEM, the authors establish Fe3Ge as a leading candidate for high-temperature spintronics.
main_problem: The study aims to observe and understand the coexistence of robust, high-temperature skyrmions and nontrivial electronic band structures in a magnetic material.
main_result: The Dirac magnet Fe3Ge was shown to host stable skyrmions up to a high Curie temperature (~650 K) while simultaneously exhibiting a large intrinsic anomalous Hall conductivity, making it a promising spintronic platform.
method: The research combines experimental measurements (magnetotransport, LTEM, magnetization) with theoretical calculations (FPLAPW, tight-binding models) to characterize the magnetic and electronic properties.
model_or_system: The physical system is the Dirac magnet Fe3Ge, which possesses a distorted Kagome lattice structure. The analysis covers its magnetic anisotropy crossover (easy-plane to easy-axis) and its topological electronic band structure.
key_observables: High Curie temperature (~650 K), large intrinsic anomalous Hall conductivity (~380 Ω-1cm-1), spin reorientation transition (~375 K), and visualization of mesoscopic skyrmions via LTEM.
important_parameters: Temperature (especially the transition points 375 K and 650 K), magnetic field strength, and the material's lattice structure (distorted Kagome).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the observed AHE is intrinsic, linked to Berry curvature, and that the observed skyrmion stability window is robust across the measured temperature range.
figures_summary: Figures detail structural characterizations (EDX, STEM), transport measurements ($ho-T$, Hall resistivity), magnetic hysteresis loops, and LTEM images showing the evolution of magnetic textures like vortices and skyrmions across different temperatures.
paper_structure: The paper systematically presents structural confirmation, followed by transport measurements revealing topological effects and anisotropy changes. It then uses LTEM and theoretical modeling to visualize and confirm the existence and stability of skyrmion phases across the temperature-dependent magnetic anisotropy crossover.
why_interesting: The combination of high operating temperature, topological electronic effects (AHE), and stable magnetic textures (skyrmions) in a single material system is highly relevant for designing next-generation spintronic devices, which often involves complex many-body interactions.
